Found live by FuzzAuthCacheDifferential (FUZZ-GAPS G5) within seconds of its first fuzzing run, not a hand-written seed. setAccountState (internal/core/account_state.go), the shared implementation behind SuspendUser/ReactivateUser/RequirePasswordReset/etc, collected every one of the target user's session AND personal-access-token hashes and evicted them from the HTTP auth cache via customMiddleware.InvalidateTokenCacheByHash for EVERY account-state transition, including a transition INTO plain active (ReactivateUser) -- but InvalidateTokenCacheByHash does not do a plain delete; per its own doc comment it writes a short-lived NEGATIVE tombstone so an in-flight positive validation racing a real revoke can't resurrect a stale entry. Writing that tombstone unconditionally meant a personal access token created WHILE an account is suspended, then swept by that SAME account's later reactivation, was spuriously rejected (401) for up to invalidTokenTTL even though it had never been cached before and the account was already active again -- oracle: the auth decision computed with the cache disagreed with the decision computed with the cache bypassed, for a token neither revoked nor expired. Fixed by scoping the proactive eviction sweep to only run when the TARGET state is more restrictive than plain active (AccountLoginBlocked || AccountRestricted) -- moving toward active never needed a proactive evict for correctness: an over-restrictive stale cache entry is safe (fail-closed), and any EXISTING positive entry already gets AccountState/Restricted refreshed on every hit by serveAuthCacheHit's own re-check, independent of this sweep. Red-before/green-after proving test creates a PAT while suspended, reactivates, and asserts the PAT authenticates on its very first use.

validateAdminDSNHost (internal/core/dynamic_secrets.go) silently skipped SSRF validation for an ENTIRE PostgreSQL multi-host admin_dsn the moment any one host in the comma-separated list was a bracket-quoted IPv6 literal (RFC 3986 requires the brackets, and PostgreSQL's own multi-host URI syntax permits mixing bracketed-IPv6 and plain-IPv4 hosts in one list, e.g. postgres://user@8.8.8.8:5432,[64:ff9b::169.254.169.254]:5432/db). Go's net/url.Parse rejects that shape outright (treats everything after the closing bracket as a single port component and errors the moment it isn't pure digits: invalid port ":5432,[...]" after host) even though pgx.ParseConfig -- the actual driver dialPostgres (internal/dynamic/postgres.go) uses -- parses and connects to it without complaint (confirmed directly against both). parseDSNHostsFromURL's only path returned (nil, false) on that url.Parse error, parseDSNHosts then found no other format match, and validateAdminDSNHost's "unrecognised format, can't extract host" branch treated the WHOLE DSN as unvalidatable -- a NAT64/6to4/Teredo/native-IPv6-encoded private or cloud-IMDS host anywhere in such a list sailed through registration completely unchecked while pgx would actually dial it. Found live by FuzzSSRFGuardDifferential, a new differential fuzzer driving one address through every independent SSRF guard in the codebase (netutil.IsPrivateOrLinkLocal/IsLinkLocal, the SIEM forwarder's and notification-channel webhook guard's own disallow policies, the connect/OIDC-JWKS Dialer{Disallow: IsLinkLocal} wiring, and validateAdminDSNHost) for encoding-parity and multi-host-DSN coverage neither FuzzIPv4EmbeddingSSRFParity nor FuzzAdminDSNHostSSRFGuard's own documented follow-up gap covered. Fixed by manualAuthorityHosts, a url.Parse-independent fallback that extracts the host-list authority segment by direct string scanning (bypassing url.Parse's authority grammar entirely) whenever url.Parse itself rejects the DSN; splitDSNHostList was also hardened to strip stray brackets from a port-less bracketed IPv6 entry. Red-before/green-after: reverting manualAuthorityHosts to return nil, false reproduces the bypass on 6 of 10 fuzz seeds (MULTI-HOST SSRF BYPASS (validateAdminDSNHost, URL multi-host): wantPrivate=true ... err=<nil>); restoring it returns all seeds plus the retained corpus entry to PASS. See the PR body for full red-proof output.

admin restore was index-blind to WHEN a backup was taken relative to subsequent legitimate changes: restoring an archive older than what this host had already certified silently resurrected any access revoked since (a suspended account, a deleted machine credential, a rotated role grant) -- the restored database simply does not know the revocation happened, and verify-audit correctly reports the restored (shorter, self-consistent) chain as VALID either way, since a bare hash-chain re-walk cannot distinguish "shorter but genuinely older" from "truncated." design-b3-backup-v2.md section 6.3 implements the fix: admin backup records the source install's own signed audit high-water mark (system_metadata audit_checkpoint_highwater) in MANIFEST.json; every server mirrors that same mark to a host-local witness file (.audit-highwater-witness, sibling to the database, internal/core advanceAuditHighWater) as it advances; admin restore compares the archive value against the witness value BEFORE writing anything to disk and refuses if the archive is behind, requiring an explicit --allow-rollback (which itself writes an audit event recording the override) to proceed. Red-before/green-after: TestAdminRestore_RefusesRollback_WithoutOverride reproduces the exact repro (an older backup restoring silently, verify-audit reporting VALID) when the check is disabled, and refuses it with the fix in place.

DeleteAuditLogsBefore deleted by event_time < cutoff; when id order and event_time order disagree (concurrent writers, HA clock skew) it removed a mid-chain row and VerifyAuditChain reported tampering. Now deletes only the contiguous id prefix of old rows (subset of the old delete) under the KEYAUDIT lock; INV-STORE-22. Postgres variants: TestDeleteAuditLogsBefore_InvertedEventTime_Postgres, TestDeleteAuditLogsBefore_HoldsKEYAUDITUntilCommit_Postgres (pg-gated)

AWSIAMExecutor.GenerateUpstream accepted a rotation whose CreateAccessKey response carried non-nil pointers to "" for AccessKeyId/SecretAccessKey -- the guard checked only created.AccessKey.AccessKeyId/SecretAccessKey == nil, never the pointed-to string's content; fixed by also requiring aws.ToString(...) != "" on both fields; fuzz-confirmed (#2209)

client.Encrypt (internal/crypto/awskms/awskms.go) returned a KMS Encrypt response's CiphertextBlob completely unchecked; a 2xx response with a missing/empty/null CiphertextBlob was treated as a successful wrap. kms_provider.go's generateAndWrap then persisted this empty blob verbatim to the wrapped-KEK file via securefiles.SecureWriteFileSync (which also has no length check) -- first-run startup appeared to succeed, but the persisted file was unusable on the next restart. Found by a private pre-disclosure fuzzing pass on aws-sdk-go-v2's KMS client (mirror harness, since internal/ packages are cross-module unimportable); structurally identical to the already-fixed awssm.go SecretString=="" gap (docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-awssm-empty-secret-response.md). Fixed by rejecting a zero-length CiphertextBlob as an error rather than returning it; red-before/green-after proving test confirmed by reverting the fix and re-running.

AWSSecretsManagerConnector.GetSecret returned success with "" when SecretString was present but empty ({"SecretString":""}) -- out.SecretString != nil is true for a pointer to an empty string, not just to real content; fixed by also requiring *out.SecretString != ""; found by FuzzAWSSMConnectorResponse (crasher 09de4b520b95a429, committed as a seed), fixed same PR; dedicated point test used as the proving test (not the fuzzer) so this claim has its own unambiguous test name, matching the connect-response-size-cap-aws-001/-azure-001 convention; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-awssm-empty-secret-response.md

AWSSTSEngine.Issue accepted a successful AssumeRole whose Credentials.AccessKeyId/SecretAccessKey/SessionToken were non-nil pointers to "" -- out.Credentials == nil is true only when the struct itself is absent, not when its string fields are empty; fixed by also requiring aws.ToString(...) != "" on all three fields; fuzz-confirmed (#2210)

AzureKeyVaultConnector.GetSecret had the identical defect as its AWS sibling (out.Value == nil, no empty-string guard) -- a response like {"value":""} returned success with an empty value; fixed by also requiring *out.Value != ""; the fuzzer's own oracle had the same pointer-only blind spot as the connector code, so it was strengthened too (now requires *ref.Value != ""), with a new {"value":""} seed added to lock in coverage; dedicated point test used as the proving test because FuzzAzureKVConnectorResponse is already the proving test for the unrelated connect-redirect-refusal-001 claim, and check-closures.sh's claim-name lookup does not disambiguate two claims sharing one (package, test) pair; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-awssm-empty-secret-response.md

Found live by this same fix's own 10-minute fuzz-validation burst, same createuser-best-effort-panic-002/-003 shape: RevokeBreakGlassActivationAtomic's post-commit evictUserSessionCache call (internal/core/account.go) had no panic protection -- a panic there, after the role removal + activation-revoke had already committed, skipped the LogBreakGlassRevoked audit call that follows it and surfaced as a request failure despite the state having already fully changed, oracle (a): Differing tables [UserRole AuditEvent BreakGlassActivation]. Fixed at evictUserSessionCache's own single choke point (defer/recover + SECURITY log line, matching emitAudit's existing pattern) -- closes it for its other two call sites in rbac_management.go too, not just the one the fuzzer reached it through. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry c3012b444731c557 is the permanent regression. See docs/findings/2026-09-23-FINDING-breakglass-revoke-half-commit.md. Regression-corpus fidelity note (2026-09-27): ADR-108 Phase 6 step 14c's opCatalog shrink silently retargeted this corpus file's decoded operation from "REST POST /api/v1/groups/{id}/members" to an unrelated op -- repaired by re-encoding the file's byte[0] to the same op's new index, verified to decode back to the original op/method/NthCall/kind tuple; guarded going forward by TestOpcatalogCorpusFilesTargetPinnedOps (server/faultops/opcatalog_corpus_pin_test.go).

Both break-glass revoke entry points (core.RevokeBreakGlass, backing the REST/gRPC human routes, and the /system RevokeBreakGlassActivationProxy) ran role removal and the activation-state update as two independent top-level storage calls, not one transaction -- an effect-then-error fault on RemoveRole (the DELETE lands, the call still reports failure) left the role gone but the activation still "active" and no break_glass.revoked audit event, oracle (d): Differing tables vs before [UserRole], vs reference [BreakGlassActivation AuditEvent]. Fixed by a new shared internal/core.RevokeBreakGlassActivationAtomic wrapping both storage calls in one storage.WithTransaction, called by both entry points; audit/cache-eviction moved to strictly after commit (CreateRole/UpdateRole's #1969/#1996 convention). No SAVEPOINT needed (verified against real Postgres, not just asserted): RemoveRole's tolerated "already gone" case is a zero-rows DELETE, not a genuine aborting SQL statement. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry 7c0a2492ee5d1dfa is the permanent regression (red-before/green-after confirmed by reverting the fix in the dev worktree and replaying). See docs/findings/2026-09-23-FINDING-breakglass-revoke-half-commit.md. Vault and Azure Key Vault connectors accepted a link-local configured Address (including cloud IMDS, 169.254.169.254) with no rejection at registration or dial time; fixed by validateConnectorAddressNotLinkLocal (registration, literal-IP case) plus connectGuardedDialer's netutil.Dialer{Disallow: netutil.IsLinkLocal} (every dial, including a hostname resolving to link-local); deliberately narrower than a full private-range block -- general RFC-1918/on-prem addresses stay unguarded, the on-prem deployment baseline; see docs/findings/2026-09-19-FINDING-connect-response-trust-gaps.md §2/§5

AzureKeyVaultConnector's client had no CheckRedirect override, so it followed a cross-host 301/302/303/307/308 redirect and trusted the redirected response as the secret value (credentials confirmed not to leak, but the response content was); found by response-fuzz harness construction, fixed by hardened_client.go's refuseRedirect wired into azurekv.go's client(); see docs/findings/2026-09-19-FINDING-connect-response-trust-gaps.md §2

AWSSecretsManagerConnector had no response-size bound; a gzip-bombed backend response (~2 MiB compressed) forced ~4 GiB peak heap via transparent decompression with err=nil; fixed by hardened_client.go's sizeCappedRoundTripper capping the decompressed body at connectMaxResponseBytes; see docs/findings/2026-09-19-FINDING-connect-response-trust-gaps.md §3

AzureKeyVaultConnector had no response-size bound; the same gzip-bomb shape forced ~3.6 GiB peak heap with err=nil; fixed the same way as the AWS sibling, wired into azurekv.go's client() via azsecrets.ClientOptions.Transport; see docs/findings/2026-09-19-FINDING-connect-response-trust-gaps.md §3

GCPSecretManagerConnector's real client() path inherited Google's SDK default of an effectively unbounded gRPC receive cap (grpc.MaxCallRecvMsgSize(math.MaxInt32)), unlike the AWS/Azure connectors' already-capped HTTP transport; found while ruling out a message-size cause for FuzzGCPSMConnectorResponse's CI OOM (the actual cause was a harness per-iteration leak, see docs/findings/2026-09-23-FINDING-gcpsm-fuzz-memory-and-recv-cap.md §1), fixed by appending an explicit grpc.MaxCallRecvMsgSize(1 MiB) dial default after Google's own; red/green-proved against the real grpc-go mechanism (bufconn + insecure creds), since option.WithGRPCConn bypasses dial-option processing entirely and ADC is unavailable in this environment; see §2 of the same finding doc

Third live occurrence of the -001/-002 defect shape: core.CreateProject's default-environment seeding and core.CreateProjectWithEnvs's requested-environment seeding (internal/core/catalog.go) both discarded a returned CreateEnvironment error as non-fatal (documented, intentional) but had no panic protection -- a panic on CreateEnvironment#1 propagated through CreateProject, past the already-committed Project row, producing a misleading 500 for a request that had, in fact, already succeeded (oracle (a): Differing tables: [Project]). Fixed by wrapping both CreateEnvironment calls in the same defer/recover idiom as -001/-002. See docs/findings/2026-09-22-FINDING-secret-delete-restore-dependency-emission-panic-masks-success.md. Second live occurrence of the -001 defect shape, found by a second unattended final-checks burst immediately after -001's fix landed: core.CreateUser's password-history seed and system_viewer auto-assign (internal/core/users.go) both discarded a returned AssignRole/AddPasswordHistory error but had no panic protection -- a panic on AssignRole propagated through CreateUser, past the already-committed User (and PasswordHistory) rows, producing a misleading 500 (Differing tables: [PasswordHistory User]). Fixed by wrapping both best-effort steps in their own defer/recover, same treatment as -001. Also fixed proactively (no dedicated live finding, but same root cause, single choke point every audit write funnels through): emitAudit (internal/core/service.go) now recovers a panic in its own LogAuditEvent call the same way it already handles a returned error, closing this for every c.Log*/writeAuditEvent* caller at once. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry 8ee52322e0585924 is the permanent regression for the CreateUser instance; emitAudit's fix is covered by the existing internal/core/server/http/server/grpc -race suites plus TestDirectLogAuditEventCallersAreSafe continuing to pass unchanged. See docs/findings/2026-09-22-FINDING-secret-delete-restore-dependency-emission-panic-masks-success.md

GCPEngine.Issue accepted a successful lease when generateAccessToken returned a nil error alongside an empty access_token -- the code only checked the error, never the token's content; fixed by rejecting when strings.TrimSpace(token) == ""; fuzz-confirmed (#2208)

commitNewKEKFiles' rename-dek error cleanup unconditionally deleted kek.salt.pending on ANY rename error, without checking whether the rename had actually applied first (e.g. an NFS lost-reply/retransmit ambiguity) -- orphaning the DEK (every secret undecryptable) whenever it had. Fixed by dekRenameActuallySucceeded verifying actual on-disk content before cleanup; found by FuzzFaultInjectedOperations same PR as the fix (docs/findings/2026-09-19-FINDING-kek-rotation-rename-dek-cleanup-dataloss.md). landed_commit is a placeholder pending this branch's actual merge commit

Login/RefreshToken/VerifyMFA/BeginWebAuthnLogin/FinishWebAuthnLogin/FinishWebAuthnPasswordlessLogin all checked the per-IP login-attempt budget then ran the slow credential check (bcrypt/TOTP/WebAuthn assertion) and only recorded the attempt afterward, on failure only -- a concurrent burst from one IP all observed the same under-budget count at check time and blew through the budget before the counter caught up. Fixed by moving the record (renamed reserveLoginAttempt) to run before the slow step, right after the request is well-formed, at every affected call site; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-login-lockout-mfa-recheck.md

G1 (FUZZ-GAPS) follow-up to login-rate-limit-reserve-first-001/PR #1981: that fix's own PR body flagged ConsumeSetup and BeginWebAuthnPasswordlessLogin as "explicitly out of scope" -- both shared checkLoginRateLimit's gate but never called reserveLoginAttempt at all, even pre-#1981, so unlike their six siblings neither ever contributed to the shared per-IP login-attempt budget and either could be hammered without limit, defeating the rate limiter as a brute-force/DoS throttle on those two endpoints specifically. Confirmed by FuzzLoginThrottleConcurrency (login_throttle_fuzz_test.go), a deterministic controlled-interleaving harness driving all 8 budget-sharing endpoints against a real storage-backed KeyorixCore and checking ground-truth login_attempts row counts (never wall-clock timing). Fixed by adding the same reserveLoginAttempt call, in the same position (after the minimal well-formedness check, before the slow step), to both call sites. Red-before/green-after: reverting both new reserveLoginAttempt calls made 9 of the harness's 11 corpus entries fail with "BUDGET NOT RESERVED"; restoring them passed all 11.

Logout (server/http/handlers/auth.go) blanket-mapped ANY error from core.Logout to 500 InternalError, including the ordinary case where the session was already deleted by a prior logout (a double-click, two tabs, or a client retry) -- confirmed live while building SESSION-N's N5 customer-journey test (real Keycloak OIDC login, then two logout calls with the same session cookie): the second call returned 500. Fixed by core.ErrSessionNotFound + errors.Is in the handler, returning 401 (an ordinary auth outcome) instead; TestLogout_InvalidToken_S8 tightened from accepting either 200 or 500 to asserting the now-deterministic 401. Logout has exactly one caller in this repo. See scripts/e2e/journeys/journey5_sso_login_test.go for the live end-to-end reproduction/regression.

TransitionMachineIdentity's post-commit, best-effort auth-cache eviction (internal/core/machine_identities.go) had no recover() around its MachineTokenHashes lookup, so a PANIC there (not just a returned error) unwound past an ALREADY-COMMITTED suspend/revoke, was caught by the outer HTTP Recovery middleware, and misreported a successful revoke as a 500 -- oracle (a). Found by FuzzStorageFaultOperations (server/faultops), fault=ListMachineIdentityCredentials#1/panic, crashing input ff58003231, now a permanent seed at server/faultops/testdata/fuzz/FuzzStorageFaultOperations/0134bc8cffdd0cfe. Confirmed the panic reproduces identically on the pre-existing fresh-per-call fuzz path too (not introduced by the in-flight world-reuse perf PR #2296 that found it faster). Fix: evictMachineIdentityCacheOrFlush recovers the panic and, on either a panic or a persistent lookup error after one retry, fails CLOSED by flushing every machine-token entry in the HTTP auth cache (InvalidateAllMachineTokenCache, server/middleware/auth.go) rather than silently leaving the revoked identity's credentials live in cache -- broader than a precise per-hash evict, but bounded to machine principals only (human sessions/PATs untouched) and self-healing (every machine principal simply re-validates against the DB on its next request, which correctly reflects the now-committed state). The proving test red/green-verified: fails on both halves (500 response, AND the revoked token still authenticating) with the recover() reverted, passes with it restored.

Confirmed (internal/core/mfa.go, ActivateMFA/VerifyMFACredentials) the local, non-proxy path never had this vulnerability shape to begin with: it calls c.storage.MarkTOTPStepUsed(ctx, userID, step) with step always internally computed by validateTOTPStep(secret, code) from a real cryptographic TOTP check, never accepted as a raw wire field the way the deleted proxy route did. IsLinkLocal (the narrower SSRF-target check used by the JWKS/OIDC egress guard and now internal/connect's hardened transport) did not decode NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96) or IPv4-compatible (::x) IPv6 encodings of an embedded link-local IPv4 -- only IsPrivateOrLinkLocal had that decode step (#1937/ssrf-nat64-ipv4compat-001); a NAT64-encoded cloud IMDS target would pass IsLinkLocal despite IsPrivateOrLinkLocal already rejecting it. Fixed by refactoring both predicates onto one shared matchesCIDRsWithEmbedded helper; found while implementing the Connect hardened-client link-local guard, which needed IsLinkLocal to have the same coverage IsPrivateOrLinkLocal already did

recover-admin (server/admin/recover_admin_logic.go), the one documented emergency-recovery mechanism for a locked-out admin, cleared the target account's password hash to "" with nothing to replace it. bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword (internal/core/auth.go's VerifyPasswordCredentials) fails unconditionally against an empty hash for every password, so the recovered account could never actually log back in through any documented path -- the one official recovery mechanism was itself a permanent self-DoS on admin access. Found live (design-b2-recover-admin.md's own §3 already claimed "the very first thing the recovered admin can do is log in, set a password" -- never actually true). Fixed by setting a server-generated one-time password (core.GenerateInitialCredential, the same generator CreateUserWithOneTimePassword already uses for new-user onboarding, ADR-028 Part E, hashed at core.PasswordHashCost) instead of an empty hash, printed once for the operator to relay, while keeping password_reset_required so every OTHER endpoint stays refused until a real password is chosen. Red-before/green-after proving test drives the full documented sequence through the real internal/core login/change-password code (not a re-implementation of it): recover-admin -> log in with the printed OTP -> forced password change -> log in with the new password -> confirm the superseded OTP no longer works.

F3c: RBACHandler.CreateRole's own permission-assignment loop had the same discard-and-log shape as F3a's replaceRolePermissions -- swallowed every AssignPermissionToRole error, always replying 201 regardless. Found live by coverage-batch-5's fuzz burst wiring REST POST /api/v1/roles/ into the operation catalog: a fault on AssignPermissionToRole's own actor-authority resolution produced a successful 201 with "permissions":null -- an oracle (c) fail-closed-authz violation, not just oracle (a). Fixed by making core.CreateRole run the role-row create and every AssignPermissionToRole call inside one storage.WithTransaction, propagating any failure as an error and auditing only after commit; both REST and gRPC now call this single function. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry c600067cf4d3bb8e is the permanent regression, no KNOWN-OPEN tolerance needed; see docs/findings/2026-09-21-FINDING-role-update-permission-replace-swallows-storage-errors.md

F3d: both core.UpdateRole's and core.CreateRole's final GetRolePermissions call (building the response's permission list) ran AFTER their own storage.WithTransaction committed and after audit logging -- a fault there reported an ERROR to the caller while the role update/create and its audit trail had already committed (oracle (a): AuditEvent table differs). Found live by an unattended fuzz burst smoke-testing coverage batch 6's two new /system ops (it found this instead, one call further down the already-fixed UpdateRole path); CreateRole had the structurally identical gap, fixed proactively before a second live finding. Fixed by moving each function's final GetRolePermissions read to be the LAST statement inside its own storage.WithTransaction closure, so a fault there rolls the whole operation back instead of reporting error-after-commit. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry 637f47f4387c3138 is the permanent regression; see docs/findings/2026-09-21-FINDING-role-update-permission-replace-swallows-storage-errors.md. Regression-corpus fidelity note (2026-09-27): ADR-108 Phase 6 step 14c's opCatalog shrink (removing 7 /system-proxy-only ops) silently retargeted this corpus file's decoded operation from "REST POST /api/v1/rotation-policies/" to an unrelated op -- repaired by re-encoding the file's byte[0] to the same op's new index, verified to decode back to the original op/method/NthCall/kind tuple; guarded going forward by TestOpcatalogCorpusFilesTargetPinnedOps (server/faultops/opcatalog_corpus_pin_test.go).

ParseResponse accepted a validly-signed response with bytes appended after its root element (XML epilogue) unrejected by either our own XML-DSig path or crewjam/saml's internal xrv.Validate (token-round-trip check, not document-structure check); found by the new FuzzParseResponse harness (#1889) on day one, fixed same PR via validatePostedResponseHasNoEpilogue

DeleteSecret handler (server/http/handlers/secrets_crud.go) unconditionally routed through the per-user owner/sharing permission check (userID != 0 required), so any machine-identity-authenticated caller got a misleading 500 on every delete regardless of the route's own scoped-permission gate; sibling handlers (GetSecret/GetSecretByName/GetSecretValueByRef) already had the correct isMachine bypass, DeleteSecret was the one call site missing it; found by the #1808 tranche-2 differential conformance harness (server/http/remote_storage_*_test.go, deleted ADR-108 Phase 6 step 14a) -- re-pointed at handlers_test.go's own direct DeleteSecret coverage rather than retired, since the fixed code path (secrets_crud.go, server/http/handlers, NOT the deleted proxy) is still live and still needs a proving test

DeleteSecret/RestoreSecret's shared emitDependencyLifecycleEvents helper (internal/core/secret_dependencies.go) correctly treated a returned error from its own best-effort ListSecretDependenciesForProject call as non-fatal (its own doc comment says so), but had no protection against a PANIC from that same call -- a panic propagated straight through DeleteSecret/RestoreSecret (which had already committed the delete/restore several lines earlier) and out to the real Recovery middleware, producing an honest-looking 500 that actually masked an already-successful delete/restore (oracle (a): SecretNode state changed despite a reported error). Found live by an unattended final-checks fuzz burst. Fixed by recovering from a panic in emitDependencyLifecycleEvents the same way it already handled a returned error -- log and return, never surface to the caller. Proving test is the fuzz harness itself -- corpus entry 059212c4cda84764 is the permanent regression; see docs/findings/2026-09-22-FINDING-secret-delete-restore-dependency-emission-panic-masks-success.md

AccountLoginBlocked and AccountRestricted are not the same predicate (pending_first_login/password_reset_required are restricted but not login-blocked) -- a session cache hit's pre-existing account-usability check only re-verified the login-blocked boolean, never refreshed the cached AccountState/Restricted, so a transition into a restricted-but-not-blocked state (e.g. an admin's RequirePasswordReset) stayed invisible to EnforceAccountRestriction on a cache hit; fixed by core.AccountUsabilityAndState / cloneUserContextWithAccountState; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-session-revoke-cache-race.md

serveAuthCacheHit's session branch only re-checked the owning account's state, never whether the session row itself still existed -- RevokeUserSessions and 6 sibling call sites (ChangePassword, ActivateMFA/DisableMFA, WebAuthn enrollment/removal, both setup-token-consume paths, the /system proxy's DeleteSessionsForUserExcept) could leave a deleted session authenticating via a stale positive cache entry; fixed by core.SessionLiveForToken wired into serveAuthCacheHit; found by FuzzConcurrentOpsLinearizable, landed same PR; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-session-revoke-cache-race.md

the same session-liveness chokepoint closes the ADR-039-documented cross-replica cache-staleness bound (a revoke on one replica leaving the session live on another for up to validTokenTTL) down to the next request, since SessionLiveForToken re-reads from the same shared DB every replica already writes to; two cores sharing one DB, only one with the cache invalidator wired, prove a replica that never heard about a sibling's revoke still denies on its next cache hit; see docs/findings/2026-09-20-FINDING-session-revoke-cache-race.md

IsPrivateOrLinkLocal (shared SSRF blocklist for dynamic-secrets admin-DSN dials, Azure KMS dials, validateAdminDSNHost) accepted NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96) and IPv4-compatible (::x) IPv6 encodings of private/loopback/IMDS IPv4 (e.g. 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe = IMDS 169.254.169.254); To4 folds only IPv4-mapped. Fixed by decoding the embedded IPv4 and checking it (not a wholesale-prefix block, so public NAT64 egress is preserved); found by adversarial probe building the DSN SSRF fuzzer, locked by FuzzIPv4EmbeddingSSRFParity (#1937)

UpdateShareRecord persisted with GORM Save(struct); against a share revoked on another replica after the read, Save's UPDATE matched 0 rows and its upsert fallback (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET all columns, deleted_at=NULL) resurrected the revoked share. Fixed with a column-scoped UPDATE scoped to deleted_at IS NULL that fails closed on 0 rows. Found by C-GUARD2-EXEMPT-REVIEW (#2662)
